t: Why can’t you just start paying again?
b: Being able to resume payments is the partial-claim test. An ongoing hardship is not. "The partial claim exists for borrowers who can resume the regular payment but cannot cure the arrears, that’s the statutory test. I can resume the regular monthly payment. I’m asking for the arrears to be handled under the partial claim." If you were told this, ask in writing which rule’s eligibility criteria were applied, and cite § 36.4803(d). 38 U.S.C. § 3737(a), three conditions: VA-guaranteed loan · primary residence · in default or at imminent risk of default. The same standard applied to the COVID-era program: 38 CFR § 36.4803(d) required that "the veteran indicates that the veteran can resume making scheduled monthly payments, on time and in full." Ability to resume the payment, not resolution of the hardship, in both programs, five years apart. MERGED FROM LIVE: the resolution-of-hardship condition belongs to the loan-modification rule, 38 C.F.R. § 36.4315(a)(2), not to the partial-claim rule.

t: "You don’t qualify, you’re already in foreclosure."
b: The statute makes loans in default eligible. The no-foreclosure bar is agency-added, not statutory. "The statute makes loans in default eligible, that’s the whole point of the program. The bar you’re citing is in VA’s handbook, not the law. Please cite the statutory provision that disqualifies me." § 3737(a)(3) makes loans "in default or at imminent risk of default" eligible. The "no pending/active foreclosure" bar is M26-4 Ch. 22 § 22.02 a.5 (FINAL, June 1 2026), not in the statute.

t: "You had a loan modification recently, so you’re locked out."
b: The 24-month modification lockout was written by the agency, not by Congress. "That restriction isn’t in the statute. If a prior modification was itself unaffordable or improperly offered, please explain how it can now disqualify me from the remedy Congress created." M26-4 Ch. 22 § 22.02 a.7 (FINAL, June 1 2026), not in § 3737. Verified: this criterion appears in the final chapter and not in the February 2026 draft. The draft instead required six payments since the most recent modification. The final replaced that with a flat 24-month lockout.

t: "You filed bankruptcy, so you’re not eligible."
b: Congress wrote no bankruptcy bar. The agency did. "Active bankruptcy isn’t a statutory disqualifier. If my case is dismissed or discharged, the handbook’s own carve-outs apply. Please state which subsection you’re relying on." M26-4 Ch. 22 § 22.02 a.4 (FINAL, June 1 2026), not in § 3737. Dismissed Ch. 7, dismissed or discharged Ch. 13, and discharged Ch. 7 with reaffirmation are carved out.

t: "The home isn’t in your name anymore."
b: The statute says "the borrower." The owner-of-record requirement is agency-added. "The statute refers to the borrower. The owner-of-record condition comes from VA’s handbook. Please identify the statutory basis." § 3737(a)(2) refers to the borrower’s primary residence. "Current legal owner of record" and the successor-in-interest exclusion are M26-4 Ch. 22 § 22.02 a.8 (FINAL, June 1 2026), not in § 3737.

t: "You were offered help and you turned it down." / "They were offered help and refused it."
b: Declining an unaffordable offer is not declining help. "I didn’t decline assistance. I declined one offer that wasn’t affordable. Please send the written evaluation notice for every option I was evaluated for, and the reason each was denied." Get every offer’s rate, payment, and denial reasons in writing; compare the new rate to your existing rate plus one point. 12 CFR § 1024.41 (RESPA / Reg X) loss-mitigation evaluation duties · 38 CFR § 36.4319. MERGED FROM LIVE: federal rules cap rate-raising modifications, 38 C.F.R. § 36.4315(a)(8), not more than one percentage point above the existing rate. In reported cohort cases the "assistance" offered was a modification that raised the interest rate several points, on fixed incomes, raising the payment by half or more.

t: "We have no record of that at this address."
b: "No record at this address" is not "we didn’t receive it." "Under RESPA, receipt of a loss-mitigation application triggers a written acknowledgement within five business days. Please send that acknowledgement, or confirm in writing that none was sent." Send formal notices by certified mail to the designated address, and keep proof of every other channel. Both matter. 12 CFR § 1024.41(b), written acknowledgement of a loss-mitigation application within 5 business days · § 1024.41(c), evaluation timeline. MERGED FROM LIVE: servicers keep a single designated address for formal error notices, 12 C.F.R. §§ 1024.35–.36, and a carefully worded "no record at this address" does not deny receiving the document through other active channels, including the federal loan technician.

t: "You’ll owe the whole forbearance amount in one lump sum."
b: Federal guidance told servicers the opposite, in writing, from the start. "The federal guidance issued to servicers says forbearance amounts are repaid over time and a lump sum isn’t required. Please point to the document that says otherwise." CARES Act forbearance fact sheet for FHA/VA/USDA servicers, repayment section · VA COVID-19 borrower guidance

t: "You should have known payments would balloon, you signed a disclosure." / "These families overextended themselves."
b: The written guidance said the opposite. A disclosure cannot undo what the government told servicers to do. These are federally guaranteed loans. "Please produce the specific disclosure you’re referring to, with my signature and its date. Then explain how it squares with the federal guidance stating repayment is over time and not a lump sum." These are federally guaranteed loans. Federal agencies told servicers in writing that paused CARES Act payments would be repaid over time and that a lump sum would not be required. Ask which of those written instructions my servicer followed, and when. CARES Act § 4022 · federal servicer guidance on forbearance repayment, repayment section · 12 CFR § 1024.41

t: "VA’s hands are tied, it isn’t statutory."
b: Congress wrote the authority. The exclusions were written by the agency. "The authority to act exists and Congress specifically authorized acting before the regulations were finished. Which statutory provision prohibits the relief being requested? Please cite it." 38 U.S.C. § 3737(h): "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the Secretary may, before prescribing regulations, issue administrative guidance … including any additional terms, conditions, and requirements the Secretary determines necessary." Also M26-4 Ch. 22: "Nothing in this handbook is intended to limit the Secretary’s discretion Congress provided under 38 U.S.C. § 3737."

t: "The program has launched, help is available." / "The program is available."
b: Launched is not available. Available and live, June 15, 2026. Required to be offered, November 28, 2026. "Available and required are different dates. VA issued the final policy June 1, 2026 and called the program live June 15. The same transmittal sets full servicer implementation at no later than 180 days from publication, which is November 28, 2026. Has my servicer implemented it? What is available to me before then?" VA final policy M26-4 Ch. 5 and Ch. 22, June 1 2026. MERGED FROM LIVE: M26-4 Transmittal Sheet Change 14 (June 1, 2026) sets full servicer implementation at no later than 180 days from publication, which is November 28, 2026. VA ready for servicer submissions June 15, 2026. Independently flagged by NCLC (launch-day release) and Military.com (June 19, 2026).

t: "If the bank was really in the wrong, they wouldn’t be foreclosing."
b: The mortgage industry warned the VA this would happen, in writing and under oath, before it happened. "The companies that do the foreclosing told Congress this would happen, seven weeks before the program ended. They asked the VA to fix it. This isn’t a family that didn’t pay, and it isn’t a bank acting alone." Mortgage Bankers Association white paper, December 12, 2024. MBA testimony to the House Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, March 11, 2025, in which Elizabeth Balce, asked what happens to veterans without the rescue program, answered: "the short answer is foreclosure. Period."

t: "You were in review, so you weren’t really being foreclosed on."
b: Both were true at once. That is what dual tracking means, and it is what the rule prohibits. "My application was pending and the foreclosure advanced at the same time. Under Regulation X those two things are not supposed to run together. Please send the dates for both." 12 CFR § 1024.41(g), RESPA / Regulation X, restricts moving for foreclosure judgment or sale while a complete loss-mitigation application is pending

t: "You can’t prove they didn’t send it."
b: You don’t have to. The rule puts the record-keeping duty on them. "I’m not asked to prove a negative. You’re required to keep the record and produce it. Please send the acknowledgement, the evaluation notice, and the upload log." RESPA / Regulation X acknowledgement and notice requirements. Servicers must maintain and produce the servicing file on a Qualified Written Request.

t: "The partial claim is a benefit you’re not entitled to."
b: VA has written the program as discretionary, not a benefit, and not judicially reviewable. Families should know that before they rely on an appeal. "I understand VA treats this as discretionary and not reviewable. I am asking for the denial in writing with the specific criterion cited, so the record is complete regardless of the review posture." M26-4 Ch. 22 § 22.01(b) (FINAL): the authority "is fully discretionary and is not a home loan benefit." 38 U.S.C. § 3737 provides that a decision under the section is not subject to judicial review and, for § 511 purposes, is not treated as a decision under a law affecting the provision of benefits.

t: "Nothing changed between the draft and the final."
b: Two of the most exclusionary criteria were added after the comment window closed. "The criteria in the final are not the criteria that were open for comment. Two of them were added afterward." February 2026 draft Chapter 22 compared against the June 1, 2026 final. The draft required six payments since the most recent modification; the final replaced that with a flat 24-month modification lockout (a.7). The final added a.10, extending the bar to COVID-19 partial claims and Refund Modifications. Neither appears in the draft.

t: "The servicer was only following the rules."
b: Servicers were bound by federal servicing law the entire time. Request the written denial notice for each option. The law requires a specific reason per option. Only the numbered 2026 waterfall is new. Regulation X, binding the entire time, required servicers to evaluate a complete application against all options within 30 days (12 C.F.R. § 1024.41(c)(1)), give a specific reason for each denial (§ 1024.41(d)), and observe the dual-tracking restriction (§ 1024.41(g)). 38 C.F.R. § 36.4319(a) carries the VA-side duty.

t: "Nobody was checking on the servicers."
b: The agency built a system to determine servicer compliance. The question is whether the servicer reported into it. The one question every oversight office can ask: produce the VALERI event history. VA built VALERI specifically to track servicer loss-mitigation compliance and inspects servicer files: M26-4 Ch. 5 § 5.11; 38 C.F.R. § 36.4350(j). "We cannot determine compliance" and "the servicer never reported into the system we built to determine compliance" are different statements.

t: "The VA isn’t the one foreclosing."
b: The Department is the named plaintiff evicting veteran families. Ask your Member: who is the named plaintiff in these evictions, and under what disposition authority (38 U.S.C. § 3732) could the VA choose otherwise? Roughly three of four foreclosed veteran homes are conveyed to the VA (Auction.com data); title passes to the Secretary of Veterans Affairs; post-foreclosure evictions are then filed in the Secretary’s name and executed through the VA’s private REO contractor. 38 U.S.C. § 3732 is the disposition authority under which VA could choose otherwise.

t: "VASP was cancelled because it was illegal."
b: No neutral body ever found VASP unlawful, and the VA itself called the authority "existing." Read the authority analysis on the Policy and Fiscal page. Then ask which neutral body made the finding, and when. VA’s own April 2024 launch materials stated it had "existing authority to establish and implement VASP under 38 U.S.C. § 3732 and § 3720." No GAO opinion, CRS analysis, OGC memo, or court ruling ever held otherwise. 38 U.S.C. § 3737(h) separately authorises acting before regulations are prescribed.

t: "Helping them would cost taxpayers more."
b: Prevention was the cheap option, by the government’s own math. See the fiscal two-path on the Policy and Fiscal page: the foreclosure path costs more than the partial-claim path, and CBO scored it. The multi-billion figures cited are gross loan-purchase volume, not net cost, buying a re-performing loan is an asset offset by repayments. CBO scored the replacement partial-claim law as reducing net direct spending by $147 million, including $294 million in offsets.

t: "Homeowners have more legal protection than renters."
b: After a foreclosure sale, the former owner usually has less protection than a tenant in the same building. "In Washington a tenant in a foreclosed property gets sixty days' written notice, and that section says it does not apply if the borrower or grantor stays on the property. The purchaser gets possession on the twentieth day. The appointed-counsel statute is written for an indigent tenant and is subject to available appropriations. I am the former owner, so I have twenty days and I should not count on counsel." In Washington a tenant in a foreclosed property gets sixty days' written notice to vacate under RCW 61.24.146, and that section says in terms that it does not apply if the borrower or grantor remains on the property. RCW 61.24.060(1) gives the purchaser possession on the twentieth day as against the borrower and grantor and occupants who are not tenants. The appointed-counsel provision, RCW 59.18.640(1), is written for an indigent TENANT in unlawful detainer proceedings under chapters 59.18, 59.12 and 59.20, and it is expressly SUBJECT TO THE AVAILABILITY OF AMOUNTS APPROPRIATED FOR THIS SPECIFIC PURPOSE. So the notice protection excludes the former owner on the face of the statute, and the counsel provision is written for tenants and is funding-contingent even for them. Wyoming has a three-month statutory redemption with the right to remain during it; Washington has none.

t: "Refer them to legal aid."
b: Referral is treated as the end of the obligation. For a household still in the home after a sale, it frequently is not. "Which provider takes post-foreclosure veteran cases in my state? I need a name, not a referral line." Not a statutory claim. Describes how foreclosure-defense and eviction right-to-counsel programs are scoped: foreclosure-defense programs generally close the file at the sale, and eviction-counsel programs generally cover landlord and tenant cases. A post-sale former owner is neither.

t: "VA cannot impose a foreclosure moratorium."

Circular 26-23-25 of November 30, 2023 encouraged a moratorium on all VA-guaranteed loans through May 31, 2024, and Circular 26-24-12 extended it through December 31, 2024. VA published its reasoning both times." VBA Circular 26-23-25 (November 30, 2023) section 3 strongly encouraged a foreclosure moratorium on all VA-guaranteed loans through May 31, 2024, excepting vacant or abandoned properties. VBA Circular 26-24-12 (May 29, 2024) section 3 extended relief as a TARGETED moratorium through December 31, 2024, with four named exceptions: vacant or abandoned; borrower documented as not wanting retention or to avoid foreclosure; 210+ days no payment with no response to outreach; all retention options including VASP evaluated and none workable.

Step two: "we do everything we possibly can to keep them from that end."

b: M26-4 Ch. 22 sec 22.02 a.7: "The borrower has not received a loan modification in the 24 months preceding the date the servicer evaluates the loan under the Waterfall." One of seven criteria in 22.02 that do not appear in 38 U.S.C. 3737. Establishes that the criterion is an agency addition, not that it is unlawful. Does not establish how many families it excludes. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: The 24-month lockout runs to the date a servicer evaluates the loan, and servicers have until November 28 2026, so a family modified after roughly November 2024 is barred at the moment the program finally reaches them.
b: The lookback in 22.02 a.7 is measured from "the date the servicer evaluates the loan under the Waterfall", not from the policy date. VA's servicer FAQ sets the operational deadline at 180 days from the June 1 2026 publication, November 28 2026. Arithmetic from two published dates. Evaluation dates vary by servicer, and a family modified earlier may clear the lookback before their servicer is operational. PROJECT ANALYSIS

t: Two of the ten qualifying criteria were changed or added after the public comment window closed, so the people who commented commented on a different document.

Criterion 10, disqualifying a prior COVID-19 partial claim payment or refund modification, does not appear in the draft. Establishes that the text changed between draft and final. Does not establish why, and does not establish that any commenter would have objected. DOCUMENTED FACT

L. 119-37 sec 7307(a) replaced that with a bar applying only to a purchase under 3732(a)(2) "unless the Secretary determines the purchase would be made consistent with section 3732(d)". The companion bar in 3732(d) was left intact. Compares enacted text with amended text. Does not assert intent, does not assert that the change caused any foreclosure, and no committee report or explanatory statement examining this specific effect has been located as of 2026-08-18. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: Of thirteen recommendations one veteran family submitted on VA's draft policy, VA adopted two, and both were drafting changes rather than enforcement or remedy.
b: A public comment on the draft M26-4 Chapters 5 and 22 was filed on March 11 2026; VA acknowledged receipt by email the same day. Each of the thirteen recommendations was compared against the text of the June 1 2026 final policy. Two were adopted: the 30 percent COVID-era cap applied by reference to when a payment was missed, and a 30-day VALERI submission clock. The eleven declined are each either an enforcement mechanism that would constrain a servicer or a remedy that would reach a family already harmed. Measures one commenter's thirteen recommendations against the final text. It does not measure what VA did with the rest of the comment record, which we have not reviewed, and it does not assert that VA read or considered this comment specifically. The comment itself is held in the case file and is not published as of 2026-08-18, so the left-hand column of the table on the page is not independently checkable by a reader; the right-hand column is, against S006 and S013. PROJECT ANALYSIS

t: Federal law sets six conditions a VA refinance must meet before it can be guaranteed, and each one can be checked from a family's own closing papers.
b: 38 U.S.C. 3709 sets four of them: the lender must certify a recoupment period and schedule all fees and incurred costs to be recouped within 36 months of loan issuance (a); it must provide the borrower with a net tangible benefit test (b)(1); the new rate must be at least 50 basis points below the old one where a fixed rate replaces a fixed rate and 200 basis points where an adjustable rate replaces a fixed rate (b)(2) and (b)(3); and the loan may not be guaranteed until the later of six consecutive monthly payments made on the loan being refinanced and 210 days after that loan's first payment due date (c). 38 CFR 36.4307 adds that the new monthly principal and interest payment must be lower and caps the new loan at the refinanced balance plus authorised closing costs and a discount of no more than 2 percent. VA Circular 26-19-22 requires the lender to twice present the veteran with a comparison of the two loans, once within three business days of application and again at closing. Quotes the statute, the regulation and the circular as published. Whether any particular refinance met them is a legal question, and most of the documents that answer it sit in the lender's loan file rather than the family's. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: VA's Inspector General reported that the Loan Guaranty Service could not confirm lenders were meeting three of those requirements.
b: VA OIG Report 21-01295-149, August 23 2023, page ii: Prior to these new controls, LGY was unable to sufficiently ensure those three requirements were met. The three are fee recoupment, net tangible benefit and loan seasoning. On the reporting lenders owe VA after closing, page iii: lenders did not comply, and LGY's controls were not sufficient for obtaining compliance. The finding describes controls in place before the May 2020 controls the audit describes, and the audit sample is fiscal year 2020. The OIG made nine recommendations and VBA concurred with all nine; three were flagged as needing a VA Office of General Counsel legal opinion before a disagreement about closing costs could be resolved. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: Thousands of veterans were overcharged on VA refinances in the year those refinances multiplied nearly sevenfold.

Page ii: the OIG estimated that at least 3,200 FY 2020 borrowers were overcharged $1.6 million. Page 19: approximately 18,400 of the FY 2020 borrowers (21 percent) were potentially overcharged a total of $3 million in unsupported, unallowable or unreasonable closing costs. Both figures are statistical estimates projected from audit samples of fiscal year 2020 loans, not counts of identified individuals. The $1.6 million estimate rests on 19 sampled loans. VA and the OIG did not agree on part of the closing-cost finding. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: In 2019 VA's Inspector General found the Loan Guaranty Service did not always oversee servicers well enough for borrowers in default to get the help they were owed.

And: The audit team estimated, based on a sample review of 200 loans, that 14 percent of loans had at least one oversight deficiency. All four recommendations are recorded as Closed-Implemented, the last of them on June 23 2020. A 2019 audit projected from a 200-loan sample. Closure records that VA satisfied the OIG it had acted on a recommendation; it does not measure what happened to families afterwards. The four closure dates differ; the private appendix this row was built from records them all as June 23 2020, which the OIG dashboard does not support. DOCUMENTED FACT

Page 7 records the response: VBA strongly oppose[s] the implication that VBA did not always fully consider the effect organizational decisions would have on Veterans, beneficiaries, and their families. The memo is cross-cutting across VBA, drawing on at least four reports issued since 2018 covering home loan funding fees, pensions, personal information and medical examinations. It is not a Loan Guaranty finding and it makes no new recommendations. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: A state attorney general has already enforced against a mortgage servicer for failing to apply COVID-era protections correctly.
b: On December 17 2025 the Massachusetts Attorney General announced a $4.65 million settlement with Newrez LLC, as successor by merger to Specialized Loan Servicing LLC, under the headline AG Campbell Reaches $4.65 Million Settlement with Mortgage Loan Servicer for Unlawful Foreclosures and Deceptive Business Practices, subtitled Violations Include Failure to Correctly Implement Covid-Era Protections. A state settlement under Massachusetts consumer protection law. It is not a VA loan case, it binds no other state or company, and a settlement is not an admission. The company is named here as the subject of a published enforcement action, not as the subject of an argument. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: A federal appeals court has held that the company servicing a loan when an escrow payment comes due is the one responsible for making it.
b: Harrell v. Freedom Mortgage Corp., No. 19-1379 (4th Cir. Oct. 2, 2020), published: the person responsible for servicing the mortgage at the time a payment is due must make that payment. The opinion ties that duty to the date the payment becomes due, and reads the Regulation X standard at 12 C.F.R. 1024.17(k)(1) so that timely manner means on or before the deadline to avoid a penalty. Published Fourth Circuit precedent, binding in Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia and West Virginia and persuasive elsewhere. The company in the case name is part of the citation, not the subject of this claim. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: Washington's own financial regulator led a national mortgage servicing settlement in 2020 and charged another servicer in 2026.
b: On December 7 2020 the Washington State Department of Financial Institutions announced the finalised multistate resolution with Nationstar Mortgage LLC, doing business as Mr. Cooper: consumer redress approaching $90 million to more than 115,000 consumers in 53 states, plus penalties in excess of $6.5 million, over conduct including missed tax payments from borrower escrow accounts, failure to terminate private mortgage insurance when conditions were met, and wrongful foreclosures. DFI led the investigation alongside 52 state regulators, 51 state attorneys general and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. On April 6 2026 the same department issued a statement of charges against Newrez LLC seeking $4,175,000, alleging among other things failing to mediate in good faith during foreclosure and improperly maintained and serviced escrow accounts. State licensing and consumer protection enforcement over mortgage servicing conduct generally. Neither action is a VA loan case. The 2026 charges are allegations; a statement of charges is not a finding. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: A family whose servicer modified their loan in the previous 24 months is barred from the partial claim by a rule Congress never wrote, and the clock runs to a date the servicer controls.
b: M26-4 Chapter 22, final, effective June 1 2026, criterion 22.02 a.7, verbatim: The borrower has not received a loan modification in the 24 months preceding the date the servicer evaluates the loan under the Waterfall. The lookback therefore ends on the date of the servicer's evaluation, not on any date the family controls. 38 U.S.C. 3737(a) sets three conditions and contains no lookback of any length and no reference to a prior loan modification. The February 2026 draft had no such criterion; its criterion 7(a) asked only that a modified loan have six monthly payments since the most recent modification. Compares handbook text with statutory text. It establishes that the lookback is an agency addition and that its end date is set by the servicer, not that it is unlawful. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: Congress made the loss mitigation sequence mandatory; VA's handbook makes the foreclosure halt wait until a trial payment plan is offered.
b: 38 U.S.C. 3732(d), added by Pub. L. 119-31 section 2(a)(3) on July 30 2025, verbatim: The Secretary shall prescribe loss mitigation procedures, including a mandatory sequence in which the holder of a loan guaranteed under this chapter shall offer loss mitigation options (including an option to enter into a partial claim agreement under the VA Home Loan Program Reform Act) to a veteran, to help prevent the foreclosure of such loan. The Secretary may not purchase an entire such loan until the veteran has completed such sequence. It names no trial payment plan. M26-4 Chapter 22 section 22.03 a.2, final, verbatim: Servicers must cease initiating, continuing, or completing foreclosures on loans where a TPP is offered to the borrower. Section 22.03 a: Servicers will only offer a TPP when the qualifying criteria are met. So the halt is conditional on all ten criteria. Quotes the statute and the handbook. It establishes what triggers the halt on paper; it does not establish what any servicer did in any case, and it does not assert that the handbook is unlawful. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: VA's partial claim chapter recognises a spouse when the marriage ends or the borrower dies, and not while the household is intact.
b: M26-4 Chapter 22, final, effective June 1 2026, searched in full on 2026-08-21: the chapter contains no occurrence of the words co-borrower, caregiver or household. It addresses family circumstance only as exceptions to a rule written about one borrower: a former spouse who received the property through a divorce (22.02 a.8(a)), a surviving spouse who received it from the estate (a.8(b)), a Successor in Interest who assumed the loan before the default (a.8(c)), a borrower deployed, hospitalised or in long-term care, where occupancy is met if the property is a family member's primary residence (a.3(c)), and a co-obligor whose signature is waived because they committed domestic violence (a.9(d)). Eligibility itself is decided on one borrower and that borrower's residence. A stated negative: three words are absent from one chapter, verified by a full-text search of the final. It is a finding about the program's drafting, not about how any servicer applies it, and not about any one family. It does not assert that a caregiver spouse on the note is excluded in practice, only that the chapter never names the arrangement. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: Eleven days after VA announced the end of VASP, the mortgage industry told the Secretary in writing that thousands of veterans who might qualify had not completed the loss-mitigation sequence, and asked VA to let borrowers fix a defective application rather than deny one filed on time.
b: CHLA to Secretary Doug Collins, April 14 2025: "There are likely thousands (maybe tens of thousands) of veterans who may qualify for VASP who haven't gone through the waterfall, and many who have been told they meet VASP qualifications but have not fully submitted documents to VA (and may not be able to within two weeks)." The letter asks that "if there is key information missing from an existing application (or an issue with title, etc), VA should give the veteran and their servicer time to cure the fault if the application was submitted on time, rather than just deny the file," and requests a 60-day transition after formal publication. A trade association's letter, not a government finding, and it does not establish that VA declined any specific application. What it establishes is that the risk was put to the Secretary in writing, by the industry that would have to administer the deadline, before the deadline ran. DOCUMENTED FACT

t: 38 U.S.C. 3709, Refinancing of housing loans (recoupment, net tangible benefit, loan seasoning)
b: U.S. Congress / Cornell LII statute 2018 The federal anti-churning conditions for VA refinances. Subsection (a) requires the lender to certify a recoupment period and that all fees and incurred costs are scheduled to be recouped on or before 36 months after loan issuance. Subsection (b) requires a net tangible benefit test, a rate not less than 50 basis points below the previous loan where a fixed rate replaces a fixed rate and 200 basis points where an adjustable rate replaces a fixed rate, and limits how discount points may produce the lower rate. Subsection (c) is the seasoning rule. Enacted as section 309 of Pub. L. 115-174, the Protecting Veterans from Predatory Lending Act, May 24 2018; seasoning amended by Pub. L. 116-33, July 25 2019, to measure 210 days from the first payment DUE date. The IRRRL audit worksheet verified this citation against law.cornell.edu on 2026-06-11; subsections (a), (b) and (c) re-read and confirmed verbatim 2026-08-21.

VASP
b: Veterans Affairs Servicing Purchase, the VA program (2024–2025) that bought defaulted VA loans and re-set them to an affordable payment. Terminated May 1, 2025.

t: partial claim
b: A tool that moves missed payments into a separate, no-interest second loan so a family can resume its original monthly payment instead of paying everything back at once.

t: forbearance
b: A temporary, agreed pause or reduction in mortgage payments. It is not forgiveness; the paused amount still has to be resolved through an exit like a partial claim.

t: REO
b: Real Estate Owned, a home the lender or guarantor takes onto its own books after foreclosure. The VA takes roughly three in four foreclosed veteran homes into REO.

t: trustee sale
b: A foreclosure sale run by a trustee without a court hearing, used in deed-of-trust (non-judicial) states like Washington. Timelines are short.

t: UD
b: Unlawful detainer, the formal court eviction case a new owner files to remove occupants after a foreclosure sale.

t: loss mitigation
b: The set of options a servicer must review before foreclosing (forbearance, modification, partial claim, short sale), meant to keep families housed.

t: funding fee
b: A one-time fee charged on many VA loans. Congress and the VA have at times proposed raising it to offset the cost of other measures.
The VA handbook chapter that sets the current Partial Claim Program rules, including the VA-added eligibility barriers that are not written into the statute.

t: CBO
b: Congressional Budget Office, the nonpartisan agency that scores the budget cost of legislation. It found the permanent partial claim saves money.

t: VALERI
b: VA Loan Electronic Reporting Interface, the system the VA uses to track servicer actions and compliance on VA-guaranteed loans.

t: SSVF
b: Supportive Services for Veteran Families, a VA-funded program offering rapid re-housing and homelessness-prevention help to veteran households.

t: IRRRL
b: Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loan, the VA refinance that replaces an existing VA loan with a lower-rate one using reduced paperwork, usually with no appraisal, no income documents and no new credit check. Federal law sets conditions it must meet before VA will guarantee it.

t: seasoning
b: The waiting period before an existing loan may be refinanced. For a VA refinance, at least six consecutive monthly payments must have been made on the old loan and at least 210 days must have passed since that loan's first payment due date, whichever comes later.

t: recoupment
b: The time it takes for the money a refinance saves each month to pay back the fees the refinance cost. Federal law requires those fees to be scheduled for recoupment within 36 months, counting the fees but not taxes, escrow deposits or the VA funding fee.

t: net tangible benefit
b: The test a lender must give the borrower showing that a refinance actually leaves them better off, through a lower rate, a lower payment or a shorter term. VA requires the lender to provide it before the loan can be guaranteed.

t: TPP
b: Trial Payment Plan. A short run of reduced or trial payments a servicer asks for before a permanent option is granted. VA's servicer handbook routes the partial claim through a Partial Claim TPP event in VALERI, so the trial plan sits in the plumbing of the program even though the statute never mentions one.
